messages.author: 675a519122febddf
messages.subject: Implementing NUTS in PyMC
parts:
Hi Stan Users!

I contribute to pymc, and I'm trying to implement NUTS for pymc. I have a draft, but I am running into the problem that the variance of the samples is too high. I try to sample a normal or t distribution with stdev of 1 and I come up with a stdev of 1.07 or so (with many iterations). 

So I am interested in strategies for verifying that NUTS is correctly implemented. What kinds of tests do you guys have for NUTS? 

Also, do you have tips for implementing NUTS?

Cheers,
John

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing NUTS in PyMC
parts:
About the only strategy we've used is to look
at quantiles of the output and verify that they're
right using either chi-by-eye or a proper chi-square test).
You can also look at this paper of Cook, Gelman
and Rubin:

http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~acthomas/724/Cook.pdf

The NUTS algorithm itself is very subtle in its
boundary conditions. We're in the middle of rewriting
it right now to make it more modular and comprehensible.

Sampling t-distributions is a tricky business when we're
talking about the Cauchy, because the variance isn't finite.
You might want to look at Radford Neal's slice sampling
paper for some analysis on why it's hard in general to
deal with fat tails in samplers that move in a way controlled
by energy changes broadly construed.

- Bob

All the Stan code's open source, so you can look
at it.

The refactoring has been merged into our master
for the next release, so it looks rather different
than the code in the current release.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing NUTS in PyMC
parts:
The NUTS part itself hasn't changed.

The new code sets everything up as a proper Hamiltonian
involving a mass matrix and a step size (step size = time
interval). The old code used varying step sizes, which
is similar in effect to a diagonal mass matrix. It's
important to use a diagonal mass matrix or varying step
sizes. We haven't evaluated the full matrix enough yet to
have a conclusive answer.

The new code is a bit different in the way it does
adaptation during warmup. The reason for the change was more
consistency than anything else.

Coming down the road, we're doing RM-HMC and Geometric NUTS.
We have a ways to go with the auto-diff first.

- Bob
